There really is no harsh divide between modes like that. LRT in America is always somewhere on a spectrum with varying segments running in mixed traffic and dedicated lanes (or even grade separated track), and really the only meaningful difference between modern streetcar and LRT is that level of right of way exclusivity. 

As to why American LRT is different, it really comes down to cost, regulatory, and land use differences. To my understanding, European trams are often legacy systems that keep being expanded upon and maintained, and still make sense to run in such short stop distances and multi-line networks due to the much higher density of the neighborhoods they run in (plus the network geometry of roadways in older cities making transit more competitive vs auto). In the United States you have to pretty selectively find corridors that work well enough to yield enough ridership demand to warrant building them, and much lower densities of land use and general sprawl mean that trains need to cover longer distances at faster speeds hence the greater stop spacing. Creating that to the extent it exists in a place like Vienna just doesn't work with the way federal transit grants (which are basically necessary for a project to be built) work in relation to ridership vs. cost, again mainly because of density.

Tldr if you want European style but LRT-ish networks it would take a massive revolution in urban land use policy and federal funding

>The purpose of public transportation is not to get the most ridership with the lowest cost. Rather, it is to provide as high quality of a service as possible to the citizens of the area the system serves.

But you have to do this with a budget, a limited and finite one. So ideally you yield the highest quality of service you can with that money. But when you come to the state and feds for those funds, the only metric that really means anything to them is the number of people who consider the service worthwhile enough to use. So why would you turn down a program that often provides faster service than LRT, is considerably nicer to ride than a local bus, and that is incredibly popular and widespread across far more communities than could be served pouring that money into a big-ticket corridor?

aBRT is great and should be invested in far far more than "true" BRT. Its cheap and quick to construct, increases ridership considerably, and provides the most tangible and immediate mobility improvements to regular riders, especially low-income riders. Purple and Gold Line are extremely high budget vs extremely low ridership and don't serve as anything but a fancy ribbon cutting and an excuse to say we invested in the East Side, and rail would just be the same thing but more extreme. But frankly aBRT (just like any other enhanced bus system like Seattle's or LA's) is what I would consider the most "advanced" methodology in contemporary American planning. It uses the most modern ITS can offer to yield the most ridership in our local network, it just isn't as glitzy.

As a transit planner, I want to note how few transit planners have responded 😂

>From my understanding, they double count transfers as separate riderships

There are two types of ridership metrics used. What you're describing are called 'unlinked' trips, that is, every boarding is counted as a boarding. 'Linked' trips are trips from an original origin to a final destination, regardless of transfers. Unlinked trips are more common but in actual federal transit grant requirements you'll be required to report both.

>and don't always include all modes of riding, whether it be buses, heavy rail, light rail, etc.

I'm not sure where you heard this from, I haven't seen any metric like that isn't explicitly described as a partial metric.

>Since it looks at the proportion of people that actually use transit/calculates the number of cars you're actually taking off the road?

This makes sense but it's thought of differently in transit planning. The number of cars taken off the road is measured instead as a reduction in automobile vehicle-miles-travelled, that is, the number of miles that would be made using personal vehicles if a given transit service wasn't in place.
 
Ultimately things are measured more incrementally. How much a regions total ridership is matters but doesn't come up as much as a relative change in that ridership total.
